extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical guidance on writing and judging novels, emphasizing the centrality of story and characterization and how other aspects (plot, fantasy, space, voice, time) interact with them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspects of the novel (the seven aspects)
rubrics_metrics.description: And the aspects selected for discussion are seven in number: The Story; People; The Plot; Fantasy; Prophecy; Pattern and Rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these seven named dimensions as distinct lenses through which to examine or construct a novel; the lectures that follow discuss them individually and their interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of the critic (Eliot)
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is part of his business to preserve tradition—when a good tradition exists. It is part of his business to see literature steadily and to see it whole; and this is eminently to see it not as consecrated by time, but to see it beyond time.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic should try to view literature as a whole and beyond mere chronology and fashions; while the lecturer admits he cannot preserve or fully examine tradition, the ideal critical stance is to understand literature's continuities and its qualities independent of historical consecration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final test: affection
rubrics_metrics.description: “The final test of a novel will be our affection for it, as it is the test of our friends, and of anything else which we cannot define.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A novel’s ultimate success is judged by the reader’s emotional attachment; this subjective response is a legitimate verdict, though it must be tempered by awareness of sentimentality and other distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against sentimentality
rubrics_metrics.description: “Sentimentality—to some a worse demon than chronology—will lurk in the background saying, ‘Oh, but I like that,’ ‘Oh, but that doesn’t appeal to me,’ and all I can promise is that sentimentality shall not speak too loudly or too soon.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentimental preference is an anti-pattern in criticism and composition: be conscious when emotional liking is driving judgment or composition, and avoid allowing facile ‘I like it’ responses to substitute for rigorous aesthetic evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story is the fundamental aspect
rubrics_metrics.description: “We shall all agree that the fundamental aspect of the novel is its story-telling aspect... That is the fundamental aspect without which it could not exist.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize story (narration of events) as the minimum requirement for a novel; even when other aspects are strong, the presence of a discernible story is foundational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of story — time-sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: “The story can be defined. It is a narrative of events arranged in their time sequence—dinner coming after breakfast, Tuesday after Monday, decay after death, and so on.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A story’s core is chronological sequence; while novelists may legitimately manipulate or play with time (e.g., Sterne, Proust), they cannot simply abolish temporal sequence without risking unintelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary merit/fault of a story: suspense
rubrics_metrics.description: “Qua story, it can only have one merit: that of making the audience want to know what happens next. And conversely it can only have one fault: that of making the audience not want to know what happens next.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a story by its capacity to sustain curiosity/suspense. Techniques that renew attention (e.g., Scheherazade’s stop-mid-sentence device) are valuable; failure to do so is a fundamental flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate manipulation of time but not its abolition
rubrics_metrics.description: “These devices are legitimate, but none of them contravene our thesis: the basis of a novel is a story, and a story is a narrative of events arranged in time sequence... Gertrude Stein has smashed up and pulverized her clock... The experiment is doomed to failure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovations that alter ordering, compress or stretch time are permissible and often fruitful; experiments that remove temporal sequence entirely tend to render fiction unintelligible and valueless—beware total demolition of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story as primitive, oral, and voice-driven
rubrics_metrics.description: “A word in conclusion about the story as the repository of a voice. It is the aspect of the novelist’s work which asks to be read out loud... The story... adds something because of its connection with a voice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The storyteller’s voice matters: consider how sentences and narrational rhythm function when spoken; certain story-writing choices gain from oral delivery and appeal to the ear as well as the eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include life by values, not only life in time
rubrics_metrics.description: “Daily life... is practically composed of two lives—the life in time and the life by values... What the entire novel does—if it is a good novel—is to include the life by values as well... it pays a double allegiance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A great novel should incorporate both chronological events and qualitative, value-laden moments (intensity, memory, meaning). Avoid novels that celebrate time alone (which can produce slack emotion and shallowness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of space/place can uplift a novel
rubrics_metrics.description: On War and Peace: “They do not arise from the story... They come from the immense area of Russia... from the sum-total of bridges and frozen rivers, forests, roads, gardens, fields, which accumulate grandeur and sonority... Space is the lord of War and Peace, not time.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use setting and an expansive sense of place to generate grandeur and musical effects that transcend mere temporal narration; spatial scale can compensate for or augment the story’s time-sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters (People): novelist reveals hidden inner life
rubrics_metrics.description: “The historian records whereas the novelist must create... the hidden life that appears in external signs is hidden no longer... It is the function of the novelist to reveal the hidden life at its source: to tell us more about Queen Victoria than could be known, and thus to produce a character who is not the Queen Victoria of history.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should expose inner passions, dreams, self-communings and interior motivations—things not available in historical record. The novelist’s craft lies in imaginatively creating inner life rather than merely reporting external actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be plausible but not literal historical copies
rubrics_metrics.description: “If a character in a novel is exactly like Queen Victoria—not rather like but exactly like—then it actually is Queen Victoria, and the novel... becomes a memoir.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid turning fictional characters into thinly disguised real persons; give characters names, sexes, plausible gestures and a measure of invented interiority so they function as created beings rather than memoiristic reproductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character construction: give names, sex, plausible gestures, and consistent behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: “The novelist... makes up a number of word-masses roughly describing himself... gives them names and sex, assigns them plausible gestures, and causes them to speak... and perhaps to behave consistently.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete details (names, gender, gestures, speech) and behavioral consistency help make characters believable. Consistency need not preclude development, but incoherent behaviour undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelist’s temperament conditions characters
rubrics_metrics.description: “A novel is based on evidence + or — x, the unknown quantity being the temperament of the novelist, and the unknown quantity always modifies the effect of the evidence, and sometimes transforms it entirely.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that the author’s temperament will shape characters and events; this subjective factor is legitimate but should be recognized as a shaping, not merely a distortion, of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of basic human facts (birth, food, sleep, love, death)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The main facts in human life are five: birth, food, sleep, love and death... Does the novelist tend to reproduce them accurately or does he tend to exaggerate, minimize, ignore... ?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide deliberately how to handle quotidian facts: realistic reproduction, stylized emphasis, symbolic exaggeration, or omission each produce different effects; choices should serve the novel’s overall aims rather than be accidental.
